props.title: Last Ride
props.initialSlug: Father and son fugitives race across Australia

sections.content: Last Ride stands among the most haunting Australian father-son road movies, following Hugo Weaving's brutal yet vulnerable performance as Kev, a violent father fleeing with his young son Chook across South Australia's stark outback. The film shares DNA with other devastating Australian coming-of-age dramas like The Boys (1998) and Beautiful Kate (2009), where family trauma plays out against harsh landscapes. Director Glendyn Ivin captures the unforgiving terrain with the same eye for isolation that made Wake in Fright (1971) so memorable.

sections.content: The Australian New Wave of the 1970s established the outback as a character itself, with films like Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975) and Long Weekend (1978) using the landscape as an almost supernatural force. Last Ride continues this tradition but grounds it in gritty realism. The vast salt lakes and desert expanses become both escape route and prison for Kev and Chook, echoing similar father-son dynamics in The Road (2009) but with a distinctly Australian harshness.

Weaving's performance ranks among his finest work, far from his better-known roles in The Matrix (1999) or The Lord of the Rings (2001). His Kev is a powder keg of masculine violence and desperate love, similar to Ben Mendelsohn's character in Animal Kingdom (2010). The film's power comes from showing how toxic masculinity passes between generations in isolated communities, a theme also explored in Romper Stomper (1992) and Snowtown (2011). sections.content: Last Ride fits within a broader trend of Australian Gothic cinema that includes Mystery Road (2013) and The Rover (2014), where the outback becomes a moral wilderness. Like these films, it uses minimal music and natural sound to create tension, letting the landscape's emptiness speak volumes. The relationship between Tom Russell's Chook and Weaving's Kev recalls the complex dynamics in Somersault (2004) and Breath (2017), other Australian films that excel at depicting young people navigating adult betrayal.
